body:
Nov 8, 2026 2:50pm PT	
	

	
	Oscar Predictions: Best Casting — ‘Being Heumann’ and ‘La Bola Negra’ Found the Year’s Boldest Discoveries. Will the Academy Reward Them?
	



			
			
	
						

									Apple 
	
					


							
		
	Variety Awards Circuit section is the home for all awards news and related content throughout the year, featuring the following: the official predictions for the upcoming Oscars, Emmys, Grammys and Tony Awards ceremonies, curated by Variety chief awards editor Clayton Davis. The prediction pages reflect the current standings in the race and do not reflect personal preferences for any individual contender. As other formal (and informal) polls suggest, competitions are fluid and subject to change in response to buzz and events. Predictions are updated every Thursday.
	



	

					La Bola Negra 
									Courtesy of Movistar Plus
	




	Best Casting Predictions Commentary (Updated: Nov. 8, 2026): Casting is only in its second year as an Oscar category and if voters just default to whichever best picture front-runner had the splashiest ensemble, the whole point of the award might be flawed. One of the two films that stand out in this category sense, are “Being Heumann,” Siân Heder’s Apple drama about Judy Heumann and the 1977 San Francisco sit-in that forced the government to enforce disability rights and “La Bola Negra,” Los Javis’ Netflix epic that threads three gay men across three eras of Spain.

	For Heder’s film, casting directors Bernie Telsey and Adam Caldwell put more than 20 disabled actors on screen around breakout Ruth Madeley’s Judy, a lot of them with little or no acting experience, which is a bigger swing than any other star-studded ensemble.

	Over in Spain, Eva Leira and Yolanda Serrano delivered Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi a cast where the pop singer Guitarricadelafuente makes his acting debut alongside newcomers Milo Quifes and Carlos González, then surrounded them with legends like Penélope Cruz and a Spanish-speaking Glenn Close. That’s discovery.

	We’ll see what other films can pop in the phase one period. 

	The list of predictions in all categories can be found here.

	The Governors Awards, which will hand out honorary Oscars to Glenn Close and Ridley Scott, will take place Sunday, Nov. 15. Preliminary voting for the Oscars shortlist in 12 categories runs Dec. 7-11, with the shortlist announcement to follow Tuesday, Dec. 15. Following the close of the eligibility period on Dec. 31, 2026, nominations voting will run Jan. 11-15, 2027. The official Oscar nominations will be announced on Thursday, Jan. 21, 2027. The 99th Oscars will take place on Sunday, March 14, 2027 and will be hosted by Conan O’Brien. The ceremony airs live at 7 p.m. ET on ABC and in more than 200 territories worldwide from the Dolby Theatre at Ovation Hollywood.

title: ‘Avedon’ Review: Ron Howard’s Thrilling Documentary About Richard Avedon, the Great Photographer Who Turned Head-On Portraits Into an Art Form
description: “Avedon,” Ron Howard’s documentary about the legendary photographer, is a fantastic movie. It’s the best documentary Ron Howard has made (my favori
body:
“Avedon,” Ron Howard’s documentary about the legendary photographer, is a fantastic movie. It’s the best documentary Ron Howard has made (my favorite before this: “The Beatles: Eight Days a Week”), and it’s been edited in a way that’s so supple and artful that its technique should be studied in filmmaking classes. (The film’s editor is Andrew Morreale.) Woven through the movie are hundreds of photographs that were shot by Richard Avedon, and there’s no question that the images are stunning, but the way the movie layers them into your consciousness is nearly musical in its finesse. And that helps to tell the very large story “Avedon” is telling: how Richard Avedon changed the metaphysics of photography, shifting the way we see the world.
	

	There’s a paradox running down the center of Avedon’s work that feels as epic and tingly as the 20th century, and that is this: He was a paragon of high fashion — the world of glamour and impossible beauty — but he was also, as a maker of images, the ultimate democratic humanist. The beauty of “Avedon” is that it explains that paradox and makes those images sing. Howard interpolates old clips and interviews, placing Avedon, with his sleek command, at the center of the movie. He also talks to models and critics and media and art-world luminaries who have a great deal of import to say. They include Tina Brown, Larry Gagosian, John Lahr, Twiggy, Adam Gopnik, Hilton Als, Calvin Klein, and Avedon’s lovingly insightful son, John Avedon. James Martin, the executive director of the Richard Avedon Foundation, takes us deep into the labyrinth of Avedon’s archives, where we see the work that resulted from the 16,000 sittings he did from 1944 until his death in 2004. That’s a long time, but it still averages out to one sitting per day, Monday through Friday, for 60 years. The movie also tells the tragic story of his mentally ill sister, whom he revered, and traces his troubled marriages.
	

	“Avedon” opens with an old clip of Richard Avedon, fixing that piercing bird-eye look of his into the camera as he explains, “I can say very little about photography. I follow no rules, no laws, and no advice.” He’s totally serious about that. We then get a montage, set to the funky martial beat of Spoon’s “I Turn My Camera On,” of Avedon portraits of the famous. John Lennon. Orson Welles. Michael Jordan. Elizabeth Taylor. Groucho Marx. Twiggy (in mid-air). Anjelica Huston. Marilyn Monroe lovingly embracing Arthur Miller. Truman Capote. J. Robert Oppenheimer.

	All the images look timeless. (Avedon’s lighting makes it look as if each one was taken yesterday.) Every subject looks like what we imagine them looking like, and also different from how you’ve ever seen them. More direct and unfiltered, more intimately themselves. That’s the Avedon touch, but the magic element is that we can’t see how he achieved it. The technique is invisible. There’s a part of one that thinks, “Okay, just set up a camera and put some black-and-white film in it. Place a famous person in front of it. Encourage them to relax and ‘be themselves.’ And voilà! I could be Richard Avedon.”

	He probably would have said you’re not wrong.

	He wasn’t very interested in the technique of photography. Talk to him about f-stops and he would glaze over. His technique was in the way he approached a session. In the film, Isabella Rossellini says that other photographers tend to shoot and shoot and shoot, but Avedon would shoot an image every so often, then tell you to think of something, then shoot again, and end up with a total of maybe 10 shots. He himself explains that if you’ve booked someone for an hour, you don’t have to shoot for an hour. He says that he wastes half an hour having coffee, and then, maybe five minutes before the hour is over, he and the subject will go over to the white paper background, and the magic happens.

	The white paper! It has its source in a remarkable story. Avedon was born in New York in 1923, and when he was a kid he says that walking down a street he would blink for a moment and keep his eyes closed, to keep what he saw alive in his head. It was his way of taking pictures before he’d even gotten a camera. He entered the U.S. Merchant Marines when he was 19, securing a place in the photographic department, where he took maybe 100,000 portraits of enlisted men and other workers, all to use for ID cards.
	

	This was the photographer’s equivalent of peeling potatoes on KP duty. But Avedon began to notice something. Shooting these military mug shots against a white background, he encountered “thousands of baffled faces looking into the camera,” and he saw how the photographs revealed these people. That’s one of the startling things about police mug shots. (John Waters: “Everybody looks better under arrest.”) We see a handful of the ID photos that Avedon took, and there it is: the Avedon style. He saw that each face was different, and needed nothing else to be different. So he took what fate handed him — a thankless military assignment — and turned it into a vision. The white background equalized everything. It became his way of making each individual stand out as an individual, with literally nothing to get in the way.

	He became a head-on existential classicist, one who echoed Diane Arbus’s eye for highlighting the aspect of a person that was somehow off. The famous Avedon shot of the model Lauren Hutton with her head thrown back and her breast popping out looks as perfectly composed as a Picasso sculpture. But it was totally spontaneous; it just happened. And that’s true of all the famous and iconic gazes Avedon’s portrait subjects gave him. Those looks weren’t planned (how could they have been?).

	At the tail-end of a session in 1953, Charlie Chaplin pranked the camera by holding devil horns over his grinning face, and that became one of the most famous images Avedon ever shot. Images like that happened…and then became frozen in the hive mind’s eye. But as “Avedon” explains, part of what he was always recording was the ineffable dance between subject and artist, using each subject to express something that there was there in himself. (Chaplin wouldn’t have made those devil horns for anyone else.)

	By the time of the 1957 Hollywood musical “Funny Face,” which paired Audrey Hepburn with Fred Astaire as a magazine photographer pointedly based on Avedon, he was already becoming a legend, and he began to use his power as part of his method as an artist. In his 1957 shoot with Marilyn Monroe, pegged to “The Prince and the Showgirl,” the trick was: How could you photograph Marilyn — or, rather, how could you photograph her the way Avedon wanted to photograph her — when she had come prepared, more than anyone else alive, to be photographed? The shoot took an entire day, and it’s full of joyous photographs of Marilyn in full splendor, but the iconic shot that emerged from it was taken at the end of the day, when she let down her guard for 10 seconds, and kind of drooped, and looked a bit sad, and we glimpse, in that photograph, the real Marilyn — not necessarily the forlorn Marilyn, but the full woman behind the image. You see Norma Jean grown up.
	

	“Avedon” is full of great stories and privileged glimpses into how Avedon created some of his most famous images. And, of course, he also photographed the unfamous, like the Oklahoma oil workers he shot in 1980. He used his impish nature to coax fashion models into leaping through the air for his models-in-motion photographs. He waited around for seven weeks in Vietnam to photograph the war’s American generals, and devised singular ways to shoot the Chicago 7 and the denizens of the Warhol Factory and the residents of the new American West, in a series that was so raw and authentic no museum in New York wanted anything to do with it. (He was that far ahead of the curve.) We also hear the story of how he photographed his aging father and used that process to reconcile with him. Avedon supported his own ritzy lifestyle by doing advertising work (including the Obsession perfume TV spots that were like surrealist mini-films), but for him it was never a compromise. And we see how that could be the case. There is, over 60 years, a breathtaking continuity between his portrait work and his fashion work and his commercial work that makes it all inseparable. That’s because every photograph Richard Avedon ever took was striving for the same thing: to open your eyes.

title: Box Office: ‘Heated Rivalry’ Fans Drive Show’s Theatrical Release to $1.4 Million
description: Nearly a year after “Heated Rivalry” debuted on streaming, fans are venturing to movie theaters to rewatch the steamy romance between hockey supers
body:
Nearly a year after “Heated Rivalry” debuted on streaming, fans are venturing to movie theaters to rewatch the steamy romance between hockey superstars Shane Hollander (Hudson Williams) and Ilya Rozanov (Connor Storrie).

	The limited theatrical release, which is scheduled from Nov. 6 through Nov. 30, has generated $1.4 million from 945 theaters, according to distributor Regal Entertainment. Moviegoers were able to choose between three paired screenings (episodes 1 and 2: “Rookies” and “Olympians”, episodes 3 and 4: “Hunter” and “Rose,” and episodes 5 and 6: “I’ll Believe in Anything” and “The Cottage”), with tickets for each showtime costing $9.99. That’s less than the average movie price, which is $12.87 for standard screenings, according to research firm EntTelligence.
	

	It’s an impressive haul for a show that’s widely available to stream at home. There aren’t many points of comparison at the box office. When television shows like Netflix’s “Stranger Things” series finale or the Christian drama “The Chosen” have played on the big screen, they aired new, never-before-seen episodes. Although Netflix didn’t report grosses for “Stranger Things,” the Season 5 series finale was estimated to have earned a massive $25 million to $28 million around New Year’s Eve. However, that’s not a fair reference given the super-sized, two-hour finale was the much-anticipated conclusion to the streamer’s biggest series of all time. In any case, theatrical releases or (re-releases) of popular TV shows are all gravy for cinema operators, who are enjoying the biggest year at the box office since the onset of the pandemic. Gen Z, the target demographic for shows like “Heated Rivalry,” has been driving the movie theater resurgence.
	

	“This could become a really interesting trend, not only as a way to bring fans together but also to keep popular series top of mind during gaps between seasons, when maintaining momentum can be a challenge,” says Rentrak’s head of marketplace trends Paul Dergarabedian. “We initially thought this might be something largely confined to the faith-based space, but clearly the potential extends to virtually any series with a passionate fan base.”

	He adds, “Of course, not every television series is going to translate into a successful big-screen event, but for the right show with the right audience, movie theaters could become an exciting extension of the television experience rather than simply an alternative to it.”

	“Heated Rivalry,” based on Rachel Reid’s “Game Changers” book series, is gearing up for a second season. The Canadian-produced show was released in the U.S. on HBO Max in November 2025, although it didn’t become a word-of-mouth sensation until early 2026, when episodes reached an average viewership of more than 10 million and made instant stars out of Williams and Storrie.

	“When a series connects with audiences the way ‘Heated Rivalry’ has, we look for ways to bring it to the big screen and give fans a reason to experience it together,” Regal’s senior VP of U.S. content Brooks LeBoeuf said prior to the re-release. “It’s a chance to celebrate the story, its creators and its performances before Season 2 arrives in 2027.”

title: Taylor Swift and Karlie Kloss Reunite at Travis Kelce’s Chiefs Game Against Jets
description: Taylor Swift and Karlie Kloss attended the Kansas City Chiefs-New York Jets game at Arrowhead Stadium on Sunday, marking their first public appeara
body:
Taylor Swift and Karlie Kloss attended the Kansas City Chiefs-New York Jets game at Arrowhead Stadium on Sunday, marking their first public appearance together in years. 

	Cameras caught the model and the “Life of a Showgirl” singer sitting in a box at the Kansas City stadium, accompanied by Swift’s mom, Andrea, and dad, Scott. Travis Kelce’s mom, Donna, also appeared to be sitting behind them, among other onlookers wearing Chiefs apparel. 
	

	Swift is no stranger to Chiefs games, but this sighting is sure to delight die-hard Swifties given the two stars’ long-time friendship. Before Sunday, Swift and Kloss hadn’t been spotted together in years, though Kloss attended Swift and Kelce’s nuptials earlier this year with her husband, Joshua Kushner. The high-profile couple tied the knot on July 3 in a star-studded ceremony at Madison Square Garden, with a guest list that was also reported to include Ed Sheeran, Bradley Cooper, Zoë Kravitz, Jack Antonoff, Gigi Hadid, Dakota Johnson, Ethan Hawke, MGK, Jason Sudeikis, Hugh Grant and Camila Cabello, among a slew of other A-listers.

	Swift and Kloss first met in the early 2010s, and quickly became close friends (their relationship even inspired a 2015 Vogue cover titled “On the Road with Best Friends Taylor Swift and Karlie Kloss”). Kloss appeared in Swift’s “Bad Blood” music video that same year and was a core member of the musician’s “1989” “girl squad,” which regularly attended concerts and events together.

	In September, Swift attended the Chiefs’ first game of the season, during which she made headlines for sitting next to Tom Cruise. “She was schooling me on football. For real,” Cruise told Jimmy Fallon during an appearance on “The Tonight Show” following the outing. 
	

	Kelce is the Chiefs’ tight end and has won Super Bowls LIV, LVII, and LVIII with the team. Back in 2024, Kelce and Swift shared a much-snapped kiss on the field after the team’s third Super Bowl win.

schema.headline: Taylor Swift and Karlie Kloss Reunite at Travis Kelce’s Chiefs Game Against Jets

title: Andy Serkis Says He Was ‘Evangelical’ About Performance Capture After Playing Gollum in ‘Lord of the Rings’ but Now Accepts It’s ‘Misunderstood’: ‘If You Get It? Great’
description: Andy Serkis, who played an instrumental role in bringing the on-screen version of Gollum (also known as Sméagol) to life in “The Lord of the Rings”
body:
Andy Serkis, who played an instrumental role in bringing the on-screen version of Gollum (also known as Sméagol) to life in “The Lord of the Rings” franchise, is reflecting on the technology that helped him do so.

	Gollum, a central character in the films, is the result of both Serkis’ performance and computer-generated elements through performance capture and CGI. In a recent interview with the Times, the actor, who is currently filming “The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum,” explained that he “never really cared about” people associating him with his arsenal of digitally-altered characters. (Serkis has also lent his talents to play Kong in “King Kong” and Caesar in the “Planet of the Apes” trilogy.)
	

	“Because this technology is so misunderstood. I used to be evangelical. I’ve talked for hours about how performance capture is acting and watched eyes glaze over, but life’s too short. I calmed down. Now I just think, ‘If you get it? Great,’” he said. “Performances like Gollum are authored by an actor in the same way a prosthetics team engineered John Hurt in ‘The Elephant Man.’ But, for some reason, a performance underneath a physical mask is more understandable to some than this, which is a digital mask.”

	In May, “Lord of the Rings” filmmaker Peter Jackson weighed in on the motion-capture conversation, saying the mounting debate over AI in film is one reason Serkis hasn’t — and likely never will — win awards for playing Gollum.

	“A lot of the current environment, everyone’s so worried about AI … I don’t think a Gollum-type character or a generated character has any hope for winning any awards,” he said at the time. “Which is a bit unfair, especially in the Andy Serkis case where it’s not an AI-generated performance. It’s a human-generated performance 100% of the way.”
	

	Serkis returns as the character for “The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum,” which he is also directing. The film is scheduled to open in theaters on Dec. 17, 2027. The ensemble also sees the return of Ian McKellen (as Gandalf), Elijah Wood (Frodo) and Lee Pace (King Thranduil), in addition to new cast members Kate Winslet (Marigol), Jamie Dornan (Strider), Leo Woodall (Halvard) and Anya Taylor-Joy as an elf.

	Serkis’ memoir, “My Pressures: The Bizarrely True Story of Andy Serkis,” hit shelves on Tuesday.

title: Maya Jama Exits ‘Love Island U.K.’ as Host After 9 Seasons: ‘All Good Things Must Come to an End’
description:
“Love Island U.K.” host Maya Jama is exiting the dating series after nine seasons. Jama made the announcement on her Instagram account Sunday.

	“W
body:
“Love Island U.K.” host Maya Jama is exiting the dating series after nine seasons. Jama made the announcement on her Instagram account Sunday.

	“What an incredible era and what an unforgettable time I’ve had, it’s been far too much fun to put into words or a video,” she began her statement. “But as all good things must come to an end, it’s my time to step down as the host of my beloved Love Island.” She continued: “I’ve always believed that to truly grow, you have to take a leap every now and then, and now is my time to throw myself into something new.”
	

	Jama first joined as the show’s host in 2023, succeeding host Laura Whitmore. In the time since, her star has soared – Jama even competed on the recent second season of “Celebrity Traitors,” on which she was the only original Traitor to make it to the final episode. This year, Jama made her acting debut in the second season of Guy Ritchie’s critically acclaimed “The Gentlemen.”

	Before becoming a sought-after presenter, Jama made a name for herself as one of the youngest BBC Radio One DJs ever.

	Read her full statement here:

	What an incredible era and what an unforgettable time I’ve had, it’s been far too much fun to put into words or a video..but as all good things must come to an end, it’s my time to step down as the host of my beloved Love Island.

	Firstly, I want to thank all of the people who rooted so hard for me to host the show in the first place. I wouldn’t change a thing.

	To the fans of the show, thank you for every supportive message and every single time you’ve tuned in during my time as host, I’m forever grateful to you all. The show really does belong to the people who watch it and embrace it year after year.
	

	Biggest thanks to the incredible production team, I’ve seen firsthand how you work your asses off for months every year to bring this iconic show to life.

	I started hosting the show aged 28 and during the 9 incredible series met the most wonderful humans along the way. I’ve loved every slow-mo walk, fire pit and live show. I’ll forever be grateful for the experience.

	But I’ve always believed that to truly grow, you have to take a leap every now and then, and now is my time to throw myself into something new.

	While my own Love Island journey has come to an end, I wish the show and the team all the success in the world, I’ll be cheering you lot on from the sidelines forever. ❤️

schema.headline: Maya Jama Exits ‘Love Island U.K.’ as Host After 9 Seasons: ‘All Good Things Must Come to an End’

title: ‘I’ve Had It’ Podcast Hosts Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan Apologize for Laughing at Charlie Kirk Joke: ‘We Regret It’
description: Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan of the “I’ve Had It” podcast have issued an apology after facing backlash for laughing at a joke about Charlie Ki
body:
Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan of the “I’ve Had It” podcast have issued an apology after facing backlash for laughing at a joke about Charlie Kirk during their latest episode, released on Thursday.

	“On Thursday’s show, we laughed at a joke about Charlie Kirk. It was an insensitive joke, and we should not have laughed. We regret it, and we apologize,” they wrote in a statement shared on the podcast’s Instagram Saturday. “Whatever our political differences, there is nothing funny about gun violence. We’ve long supported common-sense gun safety reform. To that end, we’ve made a donation to Everytown for Gun Safety, the largest gun violence prevention organization in America.”
	

	During the Thursday episode, the hosts had read social media posts made following the 2026 midterm election results. They read one that said, “We’re digging up Charlie Kirk and doing it again,” and both laughed. (That segment of the Thursday episode has since been cut out, but was reshared online.)

	“We’ll keep using our platforms to fight for the safety of all Americans,” Welch and Sullivan concluded in the joint statement.

	Several of the podcasts’ advertisers have since pulled their support of the progressive comedic podcast.

	Cash App announced it was no longer a sponsor on Friday, writing, “We do not condone violence of any kind, and we are no longer sponsors of this podcast in a post on X.  Chewy put out a statement claiming it “does not sponsor or support” the podcast. It read: “We unequivocally condemn violence in all forms. The comments made by the hosts do not reflect Chewy’s values or what we stand for as a company.”

schema.headline: ‘I’ve Had It’ Podcast Hosts Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan Apologize for Laughing at Charlie Kirk Joke: ‘We Regret It’

title: ‘Passing Strange’ Comes to Pasadena Playhouse: Creators Stew and Heidi Rodewald on the Rock Musical Reaching L.A. Almost Two Decades After Tony-Winning Broadway Run
description: “Passing Strange” will seem just a little less strange to theatergoers now than it might have when it opened on Broadway in 2007 and scored big win
body:
“Passing Strange” will seem just a little less strange to theatergoers now than it might have when it opened on Broadway in 2007 and scored big wins at the Tonys, the Drama Desk Awards and the New York Drama Critics’ Circle Awards. Without naming any names, there are plenty of successful shows since then that have taken cues from the rock musical, from how it put social and racial issues up front for its fouth-wall-breaking protagonist to having a live band on stage.
	

	The only truly strange thing, maybe, at this late date? Why it took so long for the show to get an L.A. production. After all, Stew and his creative partner Heidi Rodewald used to be prominent figures on the Los Angeles music scene, as members of the critically hailed band the Negro Problem, before the development of this show took them to New York in the early 2000s. So they’ve always a loyal audience of rock fans in SoCal eagerly waiting for the show to take root here, too, on top of Angeleno theater buffs who never got to see the show back east. Now it’s finally happening, thanks to director Zhailon Levingston, who won the Tony this year for best direction of a musical for “Cats: The Jellicle Ball.” When he sat down with the top folks at Pasadena Playhouse to discuss what he might like to do here, giving “Passing Strange” its proper SoCal premiere was at the top of his list.

	Stew and Rodewald will not be performing in the show in Pasadena, as they did throughout its entire Broadway and pre-Broadway runs. (Neither will Colman Domingo, who had a supporting role, pre-fame, on Broadway. You can see all of those performances in the film version Spike Lee directed.) Vintage Trouble singer Ty Taylor stars in this production as the Stew stand-in known only as Narrator, along with Brittany Campbell (pictured above), Britton Smith and Saycon Sengbloh. Stew and Rodewald are as eager as anyone to see what Levingston has done with a project that takes elements of Stew’s real coming-of-age and sets them to rock ‘n’ roll. The pair Zoomed in with Variety to discuss the history and impact of the show, as well as reveal some projects now in the works.
	

	The two of you aren’t directly working on this Pasadena Playhouse direction, but more like watching appreciatively from afar how it’s going, right?

	Stew: Oh, yeah. No, we wouldn’t dare. Zhailon Levingston was sweet enough at one point to invite us to peek in, but he’s a total visionary, so all we could do at this point would be drag it down. First he knows the play better than we do. Secondly, if you’ve ever seen his work, like the work he did in “Cats: The Jellicle Ball,” he’s honestly the last person I would give any advice to.

	Rodewald: The way he talks about “Passing Strange” just makes us think: Whatever you’re going to do, you get it.

	Stew: As I was just telling him just a few minutes ago, it was made for him. We don’t make art for the contemporary world. The stuff that’s moved me and Heidi for the most part has always been those early morning moments when you go home with somebody and they wanna show you that they’re cool, so they put on a record that you’ve never heard before. I call that 3 a.m. music, and I think that’s what we make. I think the Negro Problem are a 3 a.m. band. “Passing Strange” is a 3 a.m. musical. It’s not something you’re gonna get fed by the mainstream, but somebody very cool is gonna turn you onto it. You don’t necessarily make a lot of money that way, but that’s not why we’re in this, obviously.

	Here in L.A., remembering your band as an L.A. band originally, I remember hearing of the show when it was first playing at the Public and then coming to Broadway, thinking that it’d be great to see when you brought it to L.A. I couldn’t have realized that would be a 22-year journey.

	Stew: I know. We didn’t either. “Passing Strange” has been done in almost every major city except L.A. It’s been done in South America; it’s been done in Europe — so, yeah, it was starting to stick out in a kind of a weird way. But, see, we’ve always had a adversarial relationship with both Los Angeles and to the L.A. press, particularly the L.A. Times. So we were sort of not surprised at all, but other people would always come to us and go, “What’s up? The play won a Tony! Why aren’t you guys in your hometown?” And we’re like, “Uh, I don’t know.” … It’s certainly nothing we’ve lost sleep over. Having a London production to me was a dream come true, so it’s all good. But the good news is that this amazing director is doing it in L.A., so who cares about time? It’s gonna be worth the wait.
	

	Going back to the very beginnings of the show, weren’t you kind of developing some kind of preliminary version of it in clubs?

	Stew: Yeah, we had this thing called “Travelogue” that we did at some places in New York, which was sort of a cabaret version of us talking about different places that we had lived and different experiences — a very primitive version in Joe’s Pub and a couple of other clubs where we did stuff in New York, and that’s when the word started to get around. We were approached by the Public Theater. We weren’t petitioning to make a play. They approached us and said, “Would you like to make it a theater (piece)?” We said no three times, and then finally said yes.

	You’ve said that Broadway was not an aspiration of yours, ever. It was not your dream come true.

	Stew: Not at all.

	Rodewald: No, and that’s why it ended up being what it is, because we weren’t thinking that way at all. We weren’t trying to please people. We were just pleasing ourselves. I think we really held onto that. … It was this crazy surreal thing. And then we did have choices of doing it a different way or being on Broadway, and we went with that. We didn’t have to go to Broadway; we could have been one of those cool shows that goes on and on forever, off-Broadway. But it wasn’t like “Oh my God, this is all we’ve ever wanted.”

	Stew: It really helped being a rock band, because I guess there must be some rock bands that get really overly excited about things, but I think a lot of rock bands are like us: we’re very jaded. Don’t forget, we’re old enough to have experienced the implosion of the music business itself. So we remember the point where people were trying to get record deals, and then we also were there when people are like, “Fuck a record deal. Let’s make the record ourselves.” Which is what we did.

	We were in the office with Lenny Waronker, talking about a record deal, and they did give us $10,000. Woo, right? And we took that $10,000 and instead of making their demos, we took that $10,000 and made our record with it. So technically our second record is a DreamWorks project, but they don’t know it. Their accountant probably knows it, but they don’t.

	At what point did you go east from L.A. to New York?

	Stew: Yeah, we were playing in New York a lot when we were touring a lot, but I guess 2000 was probably where we really started spending more time. The best thing you can do in New York is not tell people you moved there. When you’ve moved there, you tell people you’re just visiting so they treat you better.
	

	Rodewald: We haven’t talked about this in a long time. With “Passing Strange,” we get this commission, and then we’re working at the Public Theater, and they’re sending us away to do workshops and it’s like, “Wow, they’re giving us money, so we can just keep going.” In the middle of this, Stew and I are still making albums and touring, so we’re not banking everything on it; we’re just doing this other thing. And one of the great things that happened was, by the time Broadway happened, we still didn’t officially live in New York, so they had to put us up. Otherwise, how would we have done that?

	Stew: Sort of like all the luxuries we never got with a big record deal, suddenly theater people were giving it to us, and they were much nicer.

	Rodewald: At one point, we were at Sundance, and I remember looking at you and going, “They actually care! Like, no, they actually do.”

	And that was not your experience with the record business.

	Stew: I feel like record business was just a lot of suits pretending that they get you, but not really. Theater people are really into lyrics, for instance. So that for us was something very astonishing. People liked our stage show and our outlandish name and our ambitious music or whatever, but people in L.A. didn’t really say much about lyrics. Some people did, but not like press and stuff. Then suddenly we go to New York, and the theater people are like, “Whoa, we love these lyrics.”

	Also, it’s a touchy subject because I know a lot of our L.A. people feel funny about the fact that we really did have to go to New York in order to make a living from this. Because we were selling out Spaceland on Saturday night, but there was a glass ceiling, and we couldn’t get that big record deal that was no longer around, or no longer around for a band like us. That wasn’t a possibility anymore. Suddenly in New York we had a career and could make a living. It’s always weird when hometown people leave and go elsewhere, and things happen.

	I have a lot of friends, and Heidi has a lot of friends, who, back in the day, would get a big advance from a record company, and they’d be crawling the carpets with all the cocaine and Gil Turner (high-end liquor) deliveries. And the thing is, theater doesn’t give you Gil Turner money. It doesn’t give you cocaine money up front. But it does provide you with everything else you need to create. “We’re gonna send you away on a nice retreat in the cool countryside or the hills or Berlin.” They give you everything you need in assistance, but you’re not gonna become a coke addict on a theater budget. And that’s good!
	

	Rodewald: It was amazing, but kind of embarrassing, to tell peole, “Well, we have a week, and we’re working on this, and we’re getting paid fairly.”

	Stew: I wasn’t embarrassed!

	Let’s talk about the impact “Passing Strange” had on Broadway. Did you arrive at a point where you were able to recognize the influence it had?

	Stew: For sure. After us, there were two things that were very clear. One is that every show wanted to have a band on stage. That was almost immediate. And the micro thing that only theater people would know is our lighting design, which was considered so weird at the time. Our lighting designer was like, “I want to use these lights that’ve been rejected from, like, seven shows.” And we saw it, and it looked like “Liza With a Z,” and we were like, “Hell yeah, we want this.” And then suddenly everybody started copying that look once they saw it. But that stuff isn’t really that big a deal. When I say “of course we would be influential,” I don’t mean that as from an egotistical point. Obviously, when you introduce something new, artists wanna check it out and play with it.

	But I don’t think our influence was deep enough, if anything, to be honest. I still think musicals are pretty un-rocking and kind of shallow. And when they say “rock musical,” that just means there’s gonna be a scene where you hear a fuzzy guitar turned up.

	Do you know the Iggy Pop thing where he’s [at a show in Cincinnati], he’s covering the peanut butter [all over his body] and stage diving into the audience? I show that to all my theater students, and I say, “For me, this is the epitome of rock ‘n’ roll. Why? Because we don’t know what’s going to happen next, and he is in completely in that moment. He’s high as a motherfucker, but he is completely in that moment.” And that’s what we want to achieve in rock ‘n’ roll. We want to be so present and so there that you want to come there with us. And then I ask them, “Can you show me moments in musical theater that are like this?” And when they do, they are usually scenes that are not even approaching that level of nakedness and frankness and vulnerability.

	So what I try to do in my class is get people to write musicals that are more rock ‘n’ roll. And I don’t mean rock ‘n’ roll music necessarily; I mean the spirit. So when you talk about “Passing Strange’s” influence, I mean, superficially, sure. But I don’t know if it’s been deeper than that. Maybe with some shows it has. I don’t know.
	

	Rodewald: The thing that really hit us at one point… We were touring doing some shows after that, onto the next thing. We’re playing in Detroit and most of the people there were like, “Oh, I saw that show.” When you think about how many shows we’ve played live as a band across all these years, [that didn’t compare with] we then do this show where it’s 1,200 people, eight shows a week. We didn’t go on forever, but when you think of that many people, everywhere we go, they’re like, “Oh my God, I saw you on Broadway.” And yeah, a lot of people in theater will be like, “That’s from ‘Passing Strange.'” It’s really amazing to be part of that world where people have been really influenced — a lot of people.

	Stew: Most rock people who are involved in musicals are already really famous. Like Green Day. Or it’s like, “Okay, we’re big. We got nothing else to do. Let’s make a musical,” that kind of vibe. But I feel like what was really cool for us is we weren’t anywhere near that. We were indie famous, if even that. We were able to be ourselves in theater and individual in theater because of that. We weren’t trying to please any fans; we were just trying to please ourselves.

	Do you think it broke conventions as well as helped invent some new ones?

	Rodewald: I’m thinking back on different workshops over the years, these amazing workshops like Sundance. And as we’re doing the rehearsals, we’re laughing, going, “And if we were on Broadway, we would do this.” At the end of the song, everybody claps, and then the music comes back as everybody marches off the stage, just all those kinds of things. We would just laugh about it the whole time, right? We were well aware of what those things were that we did not want to do. And we had a lot of of conversations about wanting to give people a chance to clap, where we were like, “No, no buttons” —that kind of stuff.

	How much extra life do you feel the filmed version gave the show?

	Stew: The fact that Spike Lee, of all people, filmed this play, was and still is a total dream. To have our version, so beautifully shot, live on forever, has definitely helped the play live on and reach audiences that never would have seen it. After all the work we put into it, to have it filmed by the greatest music director ever was not bad at all.
	

	In a video interview you did with Spike Lee right after he filmed the last show, you indicated you were glad you were through with starring in it in certain ways, and you didn’t really imagine other people doing it. You didn’t see it being the kind of show where somebody just stepped into your role.

	I totally didn’t, yeah. I remember the very first one we saw in D.C. And I thought, “Wow, this is awesome,” because that’s the cool thing about theater — it’s just like doing a cover. You know, the best covers don’t steal completely? The best covers do their own thing. So that was what was really fun. The narrator in the first (Washington) show was completely different than me, and I thought it was fantastic. So, yeah, the different people that have done it… We got a call from Argentina, where they were doing it, and they were like, “We’re thinking about not doing ‘The Black One’ because we just feel like that’d be kind of weird with a bunch of white Argentinian actors. Are you OK with that?” And I’m like, “Yeaaaaah, I’m okay with that.” Same when they did it in Belgium. So yeah, it’s just been fun for us. Heidi said it best — it’s bitter and… what did you say?

	Rodewald: Oh, well, I feel like I say that a lot: “Old enough and bitter enough.”

	Stew: It’s “old and bitter,” but in a very fun, devil-may-care kind of way… I think we enjoy what has happened, but we never sat around and were like, “Oh my God, this is it.” Because to us, it isn’t; it’s just we just do this. This is our life.

	You don’t have a huge, active social media presence where you’re promoting yourselves, so it would be good to catch up on what you have coming up. For one thing, does the band still do concerts?

	Stew: Oh, absolutely. Negro Problem will come out with a record in ’27. And we’re constantly writing and doing things. Heidi’s writing this amazing show about Aileen Wuornos. What is it? Is it like a song cycle, or is it gonna be a actual musical?

	Rodewald: Well, the beautiful thing about it in theater is: I don’t know yet. We’re writing the songs, and then we’re gonna figure it out. But it’s not gonna be straightforward.

	Stew: And she and I have this thing called Stewdio Zero. That’s this thing where, every four months, we make a show, and we collaborate with former students of mine from The New School, from Harvard, from LaGuardia. So it’s us being the age we are, but there’s also six people that are like a third of our age on stage collaborating to make sure things stay fresh. We perform at a wonderful space in New York called Jack, which is like our home. And, yeah, we’re crazy busy. We’re making a film of this show we did on Harlem Stage called “High Substitute for the Head Lecturer.” It’s about Amiri Baraka and Allen Ginsberg. I’m working on a Broadway-bound thing on both Muhammad Ali and Thelonious Monk.
	

	Rodewald: “Broadway-bound.” That’s amazing. I love that you said that.

	Stew: Yeah, bound in the sense of like prison. And Heidi, you’re doing something else too, right? What are you doing?

	Rodewald: Well, I’m gonna be doing the Grace and Jimmy Boggs project with you.

	Stew: Oh, yeah — we just got the money for this project about these legendary activists, Grace Lee Boggs and Jimmy Boggs. We’re gonna do this really, I hope, epic live song cycle about these two truly revolutionary activists out of Detroit. They’re already well known to political people, but I hope this musical we’re gonna make about them puts them on the map. They were unapologetically radical and wonderfully charismatic people. We’re busy as fuck. And I teach at Harvard, which is insanely busy, you know?

	Are you teaching theater or music at Harvard, or both?

	Stew: Both. My class should be titled “How to Make Musical Theater That Doesn’t Suck,” but they wouldn’t let me title it that. So it’s called “Singer Plus Song Equals Story,” and I just try to get them to make musicals that are more informed by what I would consider a rock ‘n’ roll ethos, more than “let’s put on a show” kind of stuff. The students are incredible, and this is what the Stewdio Zero group does, too, that Heidi and I have with them. They kind of teach us what’s going on now, and then we get to tell them what happened. We get to tell them about this little thing we like to call the 20th century, because they know nothing about that, if you could believe.

	Rodewald: The thing that’s changed for me is… Stew insists… I used to have to say “Tony Award-winning Stew,” like, throw that in. [Stew won the Tony for best book for a musical.] And now sometimes he makes me call him “the Professor.”

	Stew: I admitted in front of a class that there was a point in my life where I didn’t know the difference between Miley Cyrus, Katy Perry, and… what’s her name, the other one? Taylor Swift. The level of eye roll that happened among my students, it was like teaching zombies. Their eyes turned white because their eyes went so far up into their head, and they groaned this zombie-like groan. I think they all had to go to the eye doctor after I said this. They just could not believe that I couldn’t tell the difference between those three. I never tell them that I still kinda can’t if I’m just listening. This is so embarrassing, because I realize that they’re all fine. They’re great. They even have songs that I like. But when someone comes up to me and goes, “Yeah, I’m really into songwriting, like John Lennon and Taylor Swift,” you know, I just… I’m not criticizing that. I know it’s okay. I’m just not there yet, you know what I mean? Maybe by the time I’m 80. I’m 65 now. When I’m 80, I think it’ll be a Taylor Swift light bulb, you know what I mean? I’m working towards it. I’m working.

schema.headline: ‘Passing Strange’ Comes to Pasadena Playhouse: Creators Stew and Heidi Rodewald on the Rock Musical Reaching L.A. Almost Two Decades After Tony-Winning Broadway Run

title: Dave Chappelle’s Charlie Kirk Joke Prompts Response from Erika Kirk: Using the ‘Destruction of a Human Life’ as a ‘Punchline Is Beyond Disgusting’
description: After Dave Chappelle joked that he feels better ever since Charlie Kirk was murdered, Kirk’s widow, Erika, has responded to those using her late hu
body:
After Dave Chappelle joked that he feels better ever since Charlie Kirk was murdered, Kirk’s widow, Erika, has responded to those using her late husband’s death as a punchline.

	“To see leftist podcasters, comedians, and commentators laugh about political assassination as though it’s entertainment and the destruction of a human life is a punchline, is beyond disgusting,” she wrote on X Sunday. “My husband, Charlie Kirk, was killed in an act of political violence, something our two children and I will live with every day for the rest of our lives.”
	

	She continued: “A culture that laughs at assassination is one of profound moral decay. It threatens the very foundation of our country and the principles that hold our democracy together. You do not have to agree with someone’s politics to recognize the value of their life. This should not be so hard. Political violence must never be something this country tolerates, excuses, or celebrates.”

	Chappelle has been receiving backlash across social media after footage from his Friday show at Madison Square Garden — which was advertised as a phone-free experience that would require devices be stored away in Yondr pouches – showed the comedian quipping about Kirk’s death.

	“I feel fucked up saying this. It’s scary being a public speaker,” Chappelle said. “Ever since that guy Charlie Kirk got murdered, and I shouldn’t say this publicly, but I feel better.” He continued: “I know I shouldn’t say that, but it’s just a feeling. I didn’t ask to feel this way…I just be driving around like, ‘Why am I in such a good mood? Oh!’”
	

	“I’ve Had It” podcast hosts Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan also came under fire recently for laughing at a joke about Kirk during a Thursday episode of their show. The two released a joint statement on Saturday, writing that they “regret it” and “apologize.”

	The conservative activist and Turning Point USA co-founder died on Sept. 10, 2025, after being shot during a college event in Utah. He was 31.

schema.headline: Dave Chappelle’s Charlie Kirk Joke Prompts Response from Erika Kirk: Using the ‘Destruction of a Human Life’ as a ‘Punchline Is Beyond Disgusting’

title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Admits Affair, Company Probing Alleged Chinese Recruitment Plot, Report
description:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
                          Admits Affair, Company Probes Alleged Spy Plot
body:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
                          Admits Affair, Company Probes Alleged Spy Plot
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 8, 2026
                            3:01 PM PST
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Nvidia's married CEO Jensen Huang has openly admitted to an affair, leading to a probe by his company into an alleged foreign recruitment plot ... according to a bombshell report.
      
    
            Jensen -- who is married to Lori Huang -- made the startling admission to employees in an internal message obtained by the Financial Times.
      
    
            The exec apparently wrote ... "I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."
      

            While he didn't name the person he had an affair with ... the Financial Times reported that top US officials claimed Jensen had a romantic relationship with a woman named Alice Huang that U.S. intelligence believed was a Chinese spy.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Both the Financial Times and New York Times cite Alice as the person listed in a classified memo alleging she was a possible recruit of the Chinese Ministry of State Security.
      
    
            Alice is an exec at Megaspeed -- which did business with Nvidia. Before his apology ... Jensen told Bloomberg News in October that his interactions with her were "related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual."
      
    
            Following Jensen's internal message about the affair ... Nvidia's board said they would begin an independent probe "in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."
      
    
            The board added in their statement ... "The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders. While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board’s inquiry will examine all available information."
      
    
            We've reached out to Megaspeed AI for comment on Alice's behalf ... so far, no word back.

Maya Jama
                          I'm Quitting 'Love Island UK'

Maya Jama
                          I'm Quitting 'Love Island UK'

                            12:25 PM PST
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Maya Jama has completely blindsided "Love Island" fans by abruptly announcing her departure from the series after nine seasons.
      
    
            The "Love Island UK" host shared on Instagram Sunday ... "What an incredible era and what an unforgettable time I’ve had, it’s been far too much fun to put into words or a video but as all good things must come to an end, it's my time to step down as the host of my beloved Love Island."
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Instagram Media.
      
    
            As you know ... Maya took over the hosting reins in 2023 for Season 9 ... before going on to host "Love Island Aftersun," "Love Island Games" and Love Island All Stars."
      

            Maya added ... "I started hosting the show aged 28 and during the 9 incredible series met the most wonderful humans along the way. I've loved every slow-mo walk, fire pit and live show. I’ll forever be grateful for the experience."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            However, Maya -- who recently starred in Season 2 of Netflix's "The Gentlemen" -- said it was officially time to "throw myself into something new."
      
    
            Best of luck, Maya!

title: Egypt Train Crash Leaves At Least 7 Killed and Over 100 Injured
description:

                          At Least 7 Killed, Over 100 Injured
body:
Egypt Train Collision
                          At Least 7 Killed, Over 100 Injured
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 8, 2026
                            8:52 AM PST
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Two trains collided in Egypt, resulting in the deaths of at least seven people and leaving over 100 injured.
      
    
            The crash went down 30 miles south of Cairo in the al-Ayyat district ... AP News reported.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The train traveling to the Fayoum province slammed into the rear of a train heading to Aswan ... resulting in a derailment.
      

            Following the wreck ... those injured were transported to nearby hospitals after emergency crews and a crane were dispatched to the area.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi wrote on X ... "I have directed state agencies to provide the necessary medical care, promptly investigate the circumstances of the accident, and hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent."
      
    
            This latest crash comes just weeks after two high-speed trains collided in Spain, resulting in 69 deaths and more than 100 injured.
